episode_summary: The Bitcoin Podcast S02E12 (dated 2025-12-18) covers the hosts' idea of asshole-resistant technology, privacy tools under pressure from EU chat control, the 2016 DAO hack and hard fork, the practical limits of DAO governance and business-process automation, BitTorrent as an example of resilient networks, crypto influencer red flags such as guaranteed price targets and token vesting, and an argument about financial literacy.

cards.claim: D argued that crypto's real purpose is asshole-resistant technology that stops any single actor from taking over the system.
cards.speaker: D
cards.quote: the deeper we go into privacy tool scaling wars, blobs, L2s, the more critical world looks like the old world that we're trying to escape.

cards.claim: The hosts predicted privacy tools would become relevant to everyone as countries such as the EU pushed chat control.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: they are moving that way in many countries in the eu chat control is doing a thing

cards.claim: The hosts said the 2016 DAO attack was a re-entrancy bug, and the Ethereum community hard forked to refund everyone's money.
cards.speaker: host
cards.quote: a really cool idea they got ruined by a bug because someone found what's now called a re-entrancy bug and then the entire community of ethereum decided to hard fork to refund everyone's money

cards.claim: D said his team's attempt to automate business processes with BPMN showed that copying automation from one company to another would not work.
cards.speaker: D
cards.quote: So when it came to actually applying these things to automate the business at a grand scale and then being able to copy and paste those processes into different businesses, well, that just will never work.

cards.claim: D said people who think everything should run on a blockchain are naive.
cards.speaker: D
cards.quote: those who think all this stuff should run on a blockchain i think are a bit naive

cards.claim: D argued that for a for-profit business, DAOs are not for humans because the voting requirement reintroduces centralization.
cards.speaker: D
cards.quote: What I think is that for a business or a for-profit business, DAOs are not for humans.

cards.claim: The hosts said ConstitutionDAO was a failure because it lacked privacy.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: The Constitution DAO was a failure because it lacked privacy.

cards.claim: The hosts cited a Twitch streamer who was given 50k to trade stocks on Robinhood live with chat, and called the experiment a failure.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: when you know some dude gave you know twitch stream for his channel 50k to throw at stocks on robinhood

cards.claim: D said he once managed a friend's crypto as a favor and returned all the money after the friend refused to use a hardware wallet.
cards.speaker: D
cards.quote: And so finally, it just got to a point over the years where I was like, here's all your money back because I don't trust your stupidity.

cards.claim: The hosts said Coinbase is a centralizing layer on top of decentralized technology, useful for onboarding but not for ultimate control.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: It's a centralizing entity on top of decentralized technology and that's good for some things.

cards.claim: A host argued that users must be able to exit a platform with their funds or vote, otherwise the platform can control them.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: If you can exit with your funds or your vote or your identity or whatever it is, then that platform can't control you.

cards.claim: The hosts predicted that it would take only a flip of a switch for a bad actor to label private money as bad money for terrorism.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: it will be the flip of a switch for an asshole to say oh that crazy good private money

cards.claim: D said Napster was shut down because it had centralizing aspects, and the later networks became more resilient by fixing those attack vectors.
cards.speaker: D
cards.quote: And the Napster got shut down because it had centralizing aspects to it.

cards.claim: The hosts said the ARPANET was established in 1969 and closed in 1990.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: It was established in 1969, closed in 1990

cards.claim: The hosts said the Bitcoin white paper came out in 2008 and the client was released in 2009.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: 2008 was the white paper. 2009 was the release of the client.

cards.claim: The hosts said Bitcoin was about 10 years away from its AOL moment, meaning mass adoption.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: We're like 10 years away from the AOL moment, but early.

cards.claim: The hosts said anyone giving guaranteed price targets or secret information is full of it, and offered those as red flags for crypto influencers.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: If anybody's giving you guaranteed price targets

cards.claim: The hosts said buying a token after it is publicly listed usually means getting dumped on, because the team is funded by early sales.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: if you're buying a token after it's publicly listed you're getting dumped on more often than not

cards.claim: A host said most VCs expect a turnaround back to their LPs in one to two years, which conflicts with how tokens should be held.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: most VCs, depending on how sharky they are, they expect turnaround back to their LPs of profit in one to two years.

cards.claim: The hosts described typical ICO token lockups as usually a one-year cliff followed by four or five years of vesting.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: usually some sort of one-year cliff where nobody gets access to any liquidity for tokens

cards.claim: The hosts said Ethereum is a good example of a utility token because it fuels computation and secures the network.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: Ethereum is a really good example of a utility token. It is the thing that fuels the network.

cards.claim: The hosts said meme coins have no utility by design, so hype is the only thing that moves their value.
cards.speaker: unknown
cards.quote: If you look at any meme coin, it literally doesn't have any utility on purpose by definition.

cards.claim: D said 50 to 54 percent of Americans read at a sixth-grade level or below, a figure the hosts then tried to check against a 21 percent illiteracy figure.
cards.speaker: D
cards.quote: 50 54 percent of americans read at a sixth grade or below reading level

title: The Bitcoin Podcast S02E12 - Privacy, Scaling, & the Crypto Narrative War
